intro: This unit follows a thread of tall figures through the Hebrew Bible. Twelve scouts come back from Canaan afraid of the sons of Anak. Og of Bashan has a bed nine cubits long. Goliath steps out from Gath. Behind them all stands a rare word, Nephilim, first used in Genesis 6.

Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible and its ancient world, argued that these stories connect. He tied the giant clans to Genesis 6. He also read Mount Hermon and the land of Bashan as places with a spiritual reputation. Other readers see tall warriors, or the bold language of ancient war reports. You will meet each view and hear it fairly.

By the end you will be able to trace the giant clans from Numbers to 1 Samuel. You will compare what old manuscripts say about Goliath's height and explain what Rephaim means. You will describe Heiser's idea of cosmic geography. You will also talk calmly and fairly about the hard questions of the conquest stories.
bigQuestion: What did the biblical writers mean by giants, and why do readers explain them so differently?

title: Giants in the Land

chapters.title: Nephilim, Anakim and Rephaim
chapters.bigQuestion: Why does the Bible keep track of tall clans from Numbers all the way to 1 Samuel, and how have readers explained them?

story.title: Five Smooth Stones in the Valley of Elah
story.kicker: A shepherd boy picks up five stones, and a scholar later asks why the story says where his opponent came from.
paragraphs: The Valley of Elah is a wide, shallow valley in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem. In the story told in 1 Samuel 17, two armies camp on the slopes on either side. The Philistines hold one hill. King Saul and the army of Israel hold the other. Between them runs a dry stream bed, lined with smooth stones.

Each day a champion walks out from the Philistine camp. The text names him Goliath of Gath. He wears a bronze helmet and heavy armor. His spear has a head of iron. He calls across the valley for one man to come and fight him alone. Saul's soldiers hear him and stay where they are.

David is the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem. He has come only to bring food to his older brothers. He hears the challenge and offers to go. Saul gives him armor, but David takes it off, because he is not used to it. He goes down to the stream bed and chooses five smooth stones. He puts them in his shepherd's bag and takes his sling.

The story says David speaks of trusting God, not sword or spear. He runs toward the battle line and slings one stone. It strikes Goliath on the forehead, and the champion falls. The Philistine army turns and runs. For thousands of years, readers have told this story as the small one facing the great one.

Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, noticed one more detail. Goliath came from Gath. Years earlier, the book of Joshua says, a few of the tall Anakim were left in just three cities, and Gath was one of them. Heiser asked whether that was chance, or a thread the Bible ties through its stories of giants.
story.think: Why might a writer mention where Goliath came from? What can a place name add to a story?

lessons.title: Twelve Scouts in Canaan
lessons.mainIdea: In Numbers 13, Moses sends twelve scouts into Canaan, and they come back with fruit and with fear.
reading: Numbers 13 tells how Moses sent twelve men to scout the land of Canaan. There was one leader from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Their job was to look at the land, its towns and its people, and then report back. The text says the trip took forty days. In the valley of Eshcol they cut a cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole.

The scouts passed through *Hebron*, a town in the southern hill country. There they saw three men named Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai. Numbers 13:22 calls them children of Anak. The *Anakim* were a people the Bible remembers as very tall. Their name simply means the descendants of Anak.

When the scouts came back, they agreed the land was rich. But most of them said the towns had walls and the people were too strong. Caleb disagreed. He said Israel could go up and take the land. The rest of the story becomes an argument about what the scouts saw and what it meant.

words.d: a people the Bible describes as very tall, named as descendants of a man called Anak
an ancient town in the southern hill country of Canaan, where the scouts saw the sons of Anak
the old name for the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea

look.title: The Scouting Trip in Numbers 13
rows: Scouts who gave a hopeful report
Men who carried the grape cluster
look.prompt: Only two scouts gave a hopeful report. Numbers 14:6 names them. Who were they, and how many scouts disagreed with them?

check.q: How many scouts did Moses send in Numbers 13?
choices: Three, one for each son of Anak
check.why: Numbers 13 says one leader from each of the twelve tribes went. Forty is the number of days, not scouts.

check.q: In which town did the scouts see Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai?
check.why: Numbers 13:22 says the scouts came to Hebron, where these three children of Anak lived.

check.q: What did Caleb say after the trip?
choices: That the grapes were too heavy to bring home
That the scouts should stay forty more days
That Israel could go up and take the land
That the people of the land were too strong to face
check.why: Caleb disagreed with the fearful scouts. He said Israel was able to go up and take the land (Numbers 13:30).

lessons.title: Grasshoppers and Nephilim
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers 13:33 says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim, the same rare word used in Genesis 6:4.
reading: The scouts' report ends with a striking line. In Numbers 13:33 they say they saw the *Nephilim* there, and that the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim. Then they add that they felt like grasshoppers, and that is how they looked to those people too. The picture is of small insects looking up at very tall people.

The word Nephilim is rare. It appears in only two places in the Hebrew Bible: here and in Genesis 6:4. In Genesis 6 the Nephilim are on the earth when the sons of God take human wives. The King James Version of 1611 translated the word as giants in both places. The *Septuagint*, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, also used a Greek word for giants.

Michael Heiser argued that this is no accident. In The Unseen Realm (2015) he read Numbers 13:33 as a deliberate link. The writer, he said, wanted readers to connect the tall clans in Canaan with the Genesis 6 story. Heiser also argued that the word Nephilim is best explained from an Aramaic word for giants, not from the Hebrew verb for falling.

That raises a puzzle. If Nephilim lived before the flood, how could any be around in Moses' day? Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward. Readers answer the puzzle in different ways, and later lessons look at them.

words.d: a rare Hebrew word for a group of very tall people, found only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun by Jewish scholars around 250 BCE
a language close to Hebrew, spoken widely in the ancient Near East; parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic

look.title: The Scouts' Last Words
look.text: And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
look.cite: Numbers 13:33, King James Version (1611). Where the KJV says giants, the Hebrew says Nephilim.
look.prompt: What does the grasshopper comparison tell you about how the scouts felt? Is it describing size, feeling, or both?

check.q: Which two books of the Hebrew Bible use the word Nephilim?
check.why: Nephilim appears only in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33.

check.q: In Numbers 13:33, what do the scouts compare themselves to?
check.why: The scouts say they seemed like grasshoppers, both to themselves and to the tall people.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about Numbers 13:33?
choices: It shows the scouts never really entered Canaan
It is a copying mistake for the word Anakim
It deliberately links Canaan's tall clans to the Genesis 6 story
It proves the Nephilim were ordinary shepherds
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser read the verse as a deliberate link back to the Nephilim of Genesis 6.

lessons.title: A Bad Report?
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers calls the scouts' report a bad report, so some readers think its giant language grew out of fear.
reading: Numbers 13:32 calls the scouts' words an evil report. Many newer translations say a bad report. The scouts said the land eats up the people who live in it. In chapter 14 the whole camp weeps and talks of going back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and urge the people not to be afraid.

Because the text itself calls the report bad, some readers doubt the giant line. They think frightened scouts made their enemies sound bigger than they were. On this reading, Nephilim is the scouts' scary label, not the narrator's own description. The book of Numbers, they note, puts these words in the mouths of the fearful ten.

Heiser, and others who share his reading, point elsewhere. Deuteronomy and Joshua also speak of the Anakim as very tall, and those words do not come from the scouts. On this view, the problem with the report was the scouts' lack of trust, not an invented enemy. Readers still weigh both views, and the text leaves room to discuss each one.

words.d: the phrase Numbers 13:32 uses for the scouts' discouraging account; many translations say bad report
making something sound bigger or worse than it really is
the voice that tells a story, as opposed to the characters who speak inside it

look.title: Two Ways to Hear the Scouts
look.text: Reading A: The scouts really saw very tall people, and they described them truly. Their failure was fear and a lack of trust. Reading B: The scouts were afraid, so they made their enemies sound huge, borrowing an old and scary name from the past.
look.prompt: Find one detail in Numbers 13 and 14 that Reading A could point to, and one that Reading B could point to.

check.q: How does Numbers 13:32 describe the scouts' account?
choices: As a true and faithful report
As an evil or bad report
check.why: Numbers 13:32 calls it an evil report; many newer translations say bad report.

check.q: Which two scouts urged the people not to be afraid?
check.why: Numbers 14:6-9 says Joshua and Caleb tore their clothes and told the people not to fear.

check.q: Why do some readers think the Nephilim line was exaggeration?
choices: Numbers never mentions the Anakim at all
The scouts said the land had no people
Caleb is the one who spoke the line
The text calls the report bad, and the words come from frightened scouts
check.why: The narrator calls the report bad, and the Nephilim line is spoken by the ten fearful scouts.

lessons.title: Emim and Zamzummim
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 2 says nearby nations had their own names for tall peoples, and it groups them all as Rephaim.
reading: Deuteronomy 2 pauses its travel story to give a short history lesson. As Israel passes Moab, the text says a people called the *Emim* once lived there. They were great, many and tall like the Anakim. The Moabites called them Emim. But the text says they were also counted among the *Rephaim* (Deuteronomy 2:10-11).

A few verses later, the same thing happens in the land of Ammon. Deuteronomy 2:20-21 says the Ammonites called the old tall people there *Zamzummim*. They too were counted as Rephaim. The text says God destroyed them before the Ammonites, who then settled in their place.

So one kind of people had several names. Anakim, Emim and Zamzummim were local names, and Rephaim was the wider label. Deuteronomy explains this almost like a note on a map. Heiser read these notes as signs that the Bible's writers tracked the giant clans across the whole region, east of the Jordan as well as west.

words.d: a Hebrew word used for tall clans in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and for the dead in other books
the Moabite name for a tall people who lived in Moab before them (Deuteronomy 2:10-11)
the Ammonite name for a tall people who lived in Ammon before them (Deuteronomy 2:20-21)

look.title: A Map With Notes
look.text: Picture a map east of the Jordan River. In Moab, a small note reads: Emim, the Moabite name, also called Rephaim. Farther north, in Ammon, another note reads: Zamzummim, the Ammonite name, also called Rephaim. West of the Jordan, around Hebron: Anakim, also counted as Rephaim.
look.prompt: Why might a writer stop a travel story to explain local names? What does it tell you about the readers the writer had in mind?

check.q: What did the Moabites call the tall people who lived in Moab before them?
check.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 says the Moabites called them Emim.

check.q: In Deuteronomy 2, what wider name covers the Emim, Zamzummim and Anakim?
check.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 and 2:20 count these peoples as Rephaim.

check.q: According to Deuteronomy 2:20-21, who settled where the Zamzummim had lived?
check.why: The Zamzummim lived in the land the Ammonites later settled; the Edomites settled Seir, a different place.

lessons.title: Og and His Iron Bed
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 3:11 calls Og of Bashan the last of the Rephaim and describes his huge iron bed.
reading: *Og* was king of Bashan, a region east of the Jordan River. Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3 tell how Israel fought his army at Edrei and won. Then Deuteronomy 3:11 adds a note. It says Og alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. The text treats him as the last of an old line.

The same verse describes his bed, or bedstead, made of iron. It was nine cubits long and four cubits wide. A *cubit* was a measure from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches. So the bed was about 13 and a half feet long and 6 feet wide. The verse says it could still be seen in Rabbah of the Ammonites. That city is Amman, in Jordan, today.

Readers explain the bed in different ways. Heiser treated Og as a real member of the giant clans. Some scholars suggest the bed was a ceremonial couch, sized for display rather than sleep. Some older commentators thought the word for iron might describe dark basalt stone. Either way, the verse's main point is that Og belonged to the Rephaim.

words.d: the king of Bashan in Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy 3, called the last of the remnant of the Rephaim
an ancient measure from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches
a fertile region east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, ruled by Og in the Bible

look.title: How Big Was Og's Bed?
look.cite: Deuteronomy 3:11; feet worked out with a cubit of about 18 inches
look.prompt: A tall adult today is about 6 feet. How many of them could lie end to end along Og's bed?

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 3:11 say about Og?
choices: He was the champion of Gath
He alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim
He was the first of the Nephilim
He was a scout sent by Moses
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says only Og remained of the remnant of the Rephaim.

check.q: About how long was Og's bed, using an 18-inch cubit?
check.why: Nine cubits times 18 inches is 162 inches, about 13 and a half feet. Nine is the number of cubits, not feet.

check.q: Where did Deuteronomy say Og's bed could still be seen?
choices: In Edrei, where Og's army fought
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says the bed was in Rabbah of the Ammonites, today's Amman.

lessons.title: The Anakim Who Remained
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua 11:21-22 says Joshua removed the Anakim from the hill country, but some stayed in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
reading: The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan. Near the end of its war stories, Joshua 11:21 says Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country. It names Hebron, Debir and Anab. Later, Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak from Hebron. They are the same three names the scouts had seen.

Then Joshua 11:22 adds an exception. No Anakim were left in Israel's land, it says, except in Gaza, in *Gath* and in Ashdod. These three cities lay on the coastal plain in the southwest. In later books of the Bible, all three are cities of the *Philistines*.

Heiser saw this verse as a setup. It leaves a few of the giant clans in the very places where Israel's later enemies live. When a giant warrior comes out of Gath in 1 Samuel, Heiser argued, readers who remember Joshua 11:22 are meant to notice. Other readers see the verse as a plain record of places Israel did not take.

words.d: a Philistine city on the coastal plain, named as Goliath's hometown
a people on the southern coast of Canaan, often at war with Israel in the books of Samuel

look.title: Three Cities Left
look.text: There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained.
look.prompt: Name the three cities in this verse. Which one comes back in the story of David?

check.q: In which three cities does Joshua 11:22 say Anakim remained?
check.why: Joshua 11:22 names Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. Hebron, Debir and Anab are the places they were removed from.

check.q: Who drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron, according to Joshua 15:14?
check.why: Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, the sons of Anak.

check.q: Why did Heiser think Joshua 11:22 matters for the David story?
choices: It leaves Anakim in Gath, Goliath's hometown
It says David was born in Gaza
It shows the Philistines came from Bashan
It names Goliath as one of the scouts
check.why: Heiser pointed out that Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath, and Goliath later comes from Gath.

lessons.title: A Champion From Gath
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Samuel 17 presents Goliath as a heavily armed Philistine champion from Gath.
reading: 1 Samuel 17 introduces Goliath with care. He is a *champion*, a man who fights one-on-one for his whole army. The Hebrew phrase means, word for word, the man between, the one who stands in the space between two battle lines. He comes from Gath, one of the chief Philistine cities.

The writer lists his gear. He has a bronze helmet and a coat of scale armor weighing five thousand *shekels* of bronze. That is roughly 125 pounds. His spear shaft is like a weaver's beam, and its iron point alone weighs six hundred shekels. The long list is on purpose. It makes the reader feel how outmatched Saul's army seemed.

David's answer turns the scene. In 1 Samuel 17:45 he says, in effect, that Goliath comes with sword and spear, but he comes in the name of the LORD. Jewish and Christian readers have long read the story as trust set against might. Heiser added another layer: Goliath of Gath recalls the Anakim left in Gath in Joshua 11:22.

The Gath thread does not end with Goliath. 2 Samuel 21:15-22 tells of four more warriors from Gath. They are called descendants of the Rapha, which the KJV translates as the giant. Many scholars connect that word with the Rephaim. One of the four had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. David's soldiers defeated all four.

words.d: a warrior who fights one-on-one for a whole army; in Hebrew, the man between the battle lines
an ancient unit of weight, a little over 11 grams, later also the name of a coin
the name 2 Samuel 21 gives as the ancestor of four warriors from Gath; the KJV says the giant

look.title: Goliath Steps Out
look.text: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.
look.prompt: This verse gives Goliath's hometown and his height. The next lesson compares the height in different old manuscripts. What do you predict you will find?

check.q: What was a champion in 1 Samuel 17?
choices: A scout who spied on the enemy
A warrior who fought one-on-one for his whole army
A priest who blessed the soldiers
A king who ruled a Philistine city
check.why: Goliath is a champion, literally the man between the battle lines, who fights for his side alone.

check.q: According to 2 Samuel 21:20, what was unusual about one warrior from Gath?
choices: He came from the land of Bashan
He slept on an iron bed nine cubits long
He had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
check.why: 2 Samuel 21:20 describes a warrior of Gath with six fingers and six toes; the iron bed belongs to Og.

check.q: Which earlier verse did Heiser connect to Goliath's hometown?
check.why: Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath, the city Goliath comes from.

lessons.title: Two Heights for Goliath
lessons.mainIdea: Old manuscripts disagree on Goliath's height: about nine feet nine inches in one, about six feet nine inches in others.
reading: Most English Bibles translate the *Masoretic Text*, the standard Hebrew text. Jewish scribes called Masoretes copied it with great care. Its oldest complete copy is the Leningrad Codex, from about 1008 CE. In 1 Samuel 17:4 it says Goliath was six cubits and a *span* tall. A span is about half a cubit. That makes about nine feet nine inches.

Other old witnesses read differently. A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel from Qumran Cave 4, called 4QSamuel-a, was copied around 50 BCE. It reads four cubits and a span. Most copies of the Greek Septuagint also read four. So does the Jewish historian Josephus, writing around 94 CE. Four cubits and a span is about six feet nine inches.

Which reading is older? Scholars who practice *textual criticism*, the careful comparing of manuscripts, disagree. Some think a copyist raised the number over time. Others defend the Masoretic reading. Either way, a man about six feet nine inches tall, in full armor, would have stood far above most soldiers of his day.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called Masoretes
an ancient measure from the thumb to the little finger of a spread hand, about half a cubit
the careful comparing of manuscripts to learn how a text was copied and which reading is oldest

look.title: Goliath's Height in Four Witnesses
rows: Masoretic Text: 6 cubits and a span
Dead Sea Scroll 4QSamuel-a: 4 cubits and a span
Septuagint, most copies: 4 cubits and a span
Josephus, Antiquities: 4 cubits and a span
look.cite: 1 Samuel 17:4 in each witness; feet worked out with an 18-inch cubit and a 9-inch span
look.prompt: How many witnesses read four cubits? Does counting witnesses settle which reading is oldest? Why or why not?

check.q: What height does the Masoretic Text give Goliath?
check.why: The Masoretic Text of 1 Samuel 17:4 reads six cubits and a span, about nine feet nine inches.

check.q: Which old sources read four cubits and a span?
choices: The Leningrad Codex and the King James Version
A Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel and most Septuagint copies
check.why: 4QSamuel-a and most Septuagint copies read four. The Leningrad Codex and the KJV follow the Masoretic six.

check.q: What is textual criticism?
choices: Comparing manuscripts to learn how a text was copied
Writing new endings to old stories
Deciding whether a story is true or false
check.why: Textual criticism compares manuscripts, like 4QSamuel-a and the Masoretic Text, to trace how a text was copied.

lessons.title: Heiser's Thread From Genesis 6
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the Bible ties the giant clans of Canaan back to the Nephilim of Genesis 6.
reading: Put the verses side by side. Genesis 6:4 names the Nephilim. Numbers 13:33 says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim. Deuteronomy 2 and 3 count the Anakim and others as Rephaim. Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath. 1 Samuel 17 sends out a champion from Gath. Heiser read this chain as a thread the writers wove on purpose.

In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser argued that the giant clans were more than tall enemies to the biblical writers. He connected them to the *sons of God* in Genesis 6, whom he read as divine beings who crossed a line. In his reading, the clans stood for the lasting fallout of that rebellion. That is why, he argued, the conquest stories pay them so much attention.

What about the flood? If the Nephilim died in the flood, how could they appear later? Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward. Readers, including Heiser, have offered several answers, such as the same kind of event happening again after the flood. The text itself does not say how.

words.d: the figures in Genesis 6:2-4 who take human wives; Heiser read them as divine beings, others as human men
a being of the heavenly world, such as an angel or a member of God's heavenly council
the lasting results of an event, especially a bad one

look.title: The Chain of Verses
look.text: Genesis 6:4: the Nephilim are on the earth, then and also afterward. Numbers 13:33: the sons of Anak come from the Nephilim. Deuteronomy 2:11: the Anakim are counted as Rephaim. Deuteronomy 3:11: Og is the last of the Rephaim. Joshua 11:22: Anakim remain in Gath. 1 Samuel 17:4: Goliath of Gath steps out.
look.prompt: Which link in this chain seems strongest to you, and which seems weakest? Point to the verse and explain.

check.q: Which phrase in Genesis 6:4 helps readers explain giants after the flood?
check.why: Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward.

check.q: In Heiser's reading, what did the giant clans stand for?
choices: The lasting fallout of the rebellion in Genesis 6
check.why: Heiser tied the clans to the sons of God in Genesis 6. He rejected claims that giants built the pyramids.

check.q: Which book did Heiser write that argues for this thread?
check.why: The Unseen Realm (2015) is Heiser's book. The 1917 Book of Enoch is R. H. Charles's translation.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read the Giants
lessons.mainIdea: Many readers see the giant clans as tall warriors, or as enemies made larger in ancient war writing.
reading: Not every reader follows Heiser. One common view is that the Anakim and Rephaim were simply tall peoples. Tall families and tall warriors appear in every age. On this reading, the Bible remembers real enemies who stood out, with no link to heavenly beings.

A second view looks at how ancient people wrote about war. Kings and scribes across the ancient Near East often made enemies sound huge and victories total. Some scholars read the giant language as this kind of *hyperbole*. It shows, they say, that Israel's God gave victory against impossible odds. The scouts' bad report in Numbers 13 fits this reading too.

A third group, including many Jewish and Christian readers, reads the sons of God in Genesis 6 as human. Some take them to be men from the family line of Seth, the *Sethite view*. Others take them to be powerful rulers. For these readers the Nephilim were mighty humans. Each reading tries to explain the same verses.

Some modern books claim that giants built the pyramids or came from other planets. Heiser rejected such claims. A good check is simple: open the text and see whether it actually says so. None of these verses mention pyramids or other worlds.

words.d: deliberate exaggeration used for effect, common in ancient war writing
the reading that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were men from the family line of Seth

look.title: Three Readings, One Verse
look.text: Take Numbers 13:33. Heiser's reading: the writer links the Anakim to the Nephilim of Genesis 6 on purpose. Tall-warrior reading: the Anakim were very tall people, and the scouts named them with an old word. Hyperbole reading: frightened scouts, and later writers, made the enemy sound larger than life.
look.prompt: Pick a different verse from this chapter. How would each of the three readings explain it?

check.q: What is the Sethite view of Genesis 6?
choices: The sons of God were Philistine kings
The sons of God were men from the family line of Seth
The sons of God were giants from Bashan
Seth was the first of the Nephilim
check.why: The Sethite view reads the sons of God as human men descended from Seth.

check.q: Why do some scholars think the giant language is hyperbole?
choices: Giants appear only in the Septuagint
The Hebrew word for giant means grasshopper
Ancient war writing often made enemies sound huge
check.why: Across the ancient Near East, war reports often enlarged enemies and victories.

check.q: How did Heiser respond to claims that giants built the pyramids?
choices: He defended them in The Unseen Realm
He said Og built the pyramids
check.why: Heiser rejected ancient-astronaut and pyramid claims; the biblical texts do not say these things.

lessons.title: Rephaim: Giants and the Dead
lessons.mainIdea: The word Rephaim names giant clans in some verses and the spirits of the dead in others.
reading: Rephaim is a puzzling word. In Deuteronomy and Joshua it names tall clans. In other books it names the dead. Psalm 88:10 asks whether the Rephaim will rise and praise God, and the King James Version translates the word as the dead. Isaiah 26:14 and Proverbs 9:18 use it the same way, for those in the realm of the dead.

Clay tablets from *Ugarit* help explain this. Ugarit was an ancient city on the coast of Syria. It was destroyed around 1185 BCE, and its tablets were found from 1929 on. Its texts speak of the rpum, a word scholars connect with Rephaim. In these texts they are honored ancestors, especially dead kings, remembered in ceremonies for the royal family.

Heiser argued the two uses belong together. In his reading, the biblical writers linked the giant clans with the shadowy dead of the *underworld*, and the one word carried both ideas. Other scholars think the word simply had two meanings. Some suggest that old warrior kings came to be remembered as the mighty dead. Either way, knowing both uses helps readers of Isaiah and the Psalms.

words.d: an ancient city on the Syrian coast whose clay tablets, found from 1929 on, shed light on the Hebrew Bible
the realm of the dead; in the Hebrew Bible it is often called Sheol
a word in the tablets of Ugarit for honored dead ancestors, connected by scholars with Rephaim

look.title: A Question in the Psalms
look.text: Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah.
look.cite: Psalm 88:10, King James Version (1611). The Hebrew word translated the dead is rephaim.
look.prompt: The same Hebrew word names Og's clan in Deuteronomy. What changes when you read it here as the dead?

check.q: How does the KJV translate rephaim in Psalm 88:10?
check.why: In Psalm 88:10 the KJV renders rephaim as the dead.

check.q: Where was Ugarit?
check.why: Ugarit was a city on the Syrian coast; its tablets were found from 1929 on.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about the two uses of Rephaim?
choices: They are two unrelated words that only look alike
They were both invented by the Septuagint
They belong together, linking giant clans and the dead
check.why: Heiser read the giant clans and the dead Rephaim as linked ideas carried by one word.

review.q: Which verse says the sons of Anak came from the Nephilim?
review.why: Numbers 13:33 is the scouts' line linking the sons of Anak to the Nephilim.

review.q: What is Og called in Deuteronomy 3:11?
choices: A scout who returned with grapes
The last of the remnant of the Rephaim
review.why: Deuteronomy 3:11 says Og alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim.

review.q: The Emim and Zamzummim were local names for which wider group?
review.why: Deuteronomy 2:11 and 2:20 count both peoples as Rephaim.

review.q: How do manuscripts differ on Goliath's height?
choices: The Masoretic Text says six cubits and a span; a Dead Sea Scroll says four
Only the King James Version gives a height
All manuscripts agree he was nine cubits
review.why: The Masoretic Text reads six cubits and a span, while 4QSamuel-a and most Septuagint copies read four.

review.q: In Heiser's reading, what links Goliath to Joshua 11:22?
review.why: Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath, and Goliath comes from Gath.

review.q: Which is a reading of the giant stories other than Heiser's?
choices: They describe tall warriors, enlarged by ancient war writing
They describe the kings of Ugarit
They describe the Masoretes who copied the text
They describe the twelve scouts' families
review.why: Many readers see the clans as tall peoples, described with the hyperbole common in ancient war reports.

review.q: Besides giant clans, what else can Rephaim mean in the Hebrew Bible?
review.why: In Psalm 88:10, Isaiah 26:14 and Proverbs 9:18, rephaim means the dead.

review.q: Which ancient city's tablets speak of the rpum?
review.why: The tablets of Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, speak of the rpum as honored dead ancestors.

chapters.title: Bashan, Hermon and the Conquest
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did a mountain and a plain in the far north carry such weight in the Bible's stories, and how do readers face the hard questions of the conquest?

story.title: A View From Snowy Hermon
story.kicker: A hiker looks south from Mount Hermon and tries to see the land the way ancient writers did.
paragraphs: Early on a clear winter morning, a hiker climbs the upper slopes of Mount Hermon. Snow squeaks under her boots. Hermon is the tallest mountain in the region, about 9,200 feet high. Its peaks sit where Lebanon and Syria meet, and its southern slopes reach into the Golan Heights. Up here the air is cold and the view stretches for miles.

She turns and looks south. Below her spreads a high plain of dark volcanic rock and green fields. This is the land the Bible calls Bashan. Far off, a small blue shape catches the light. It is the Sea of Galilee. Melting snow runs down Hermon's sides and feeds the springs of the Jordan River.

At the foot of the mountain lie the springs of Banias. In New Testament times a city called Caesarea Philippi stood there. The book of Joshua tells of a much older time. It says Og, king of Bashan, ruled from Mount Hermon down across this land, from the cities of Ashtaroth and Edrei.

The hiker has a folded page of notes in her pocket. The notes are on a book by Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible. Heiser argued that for ancient readers this view was not just scenery. The mountain and the plain below it were places with a spiritual reputation. She puts the page away and looks again, trying to see the land as those old writers did.
story.think: Is there a place near you that people connect with a strong feeling or story? How does that change the way they see it?

lessons.title: Mount Hermon, the High Landmark
lessons.mainIdea: Mount Hermon, about 9,200 feet high, marks the northern edge of the land in many biblical texts.
reading: *Mount Hermon* rises about 9,200 feet at the north end of the lands the Bible describes. Snow covers its top for much of the year, which is rare in this region. Its melting snow feeds springs that become the Jordan River. For people far to the south, it was the great white mountain on the horizon.

Hermon had more than one name. Deuteronomy 3:9 says the Sidonians called it Sirion and the Amorites called it Senir; the King James Version spells it Shenir. Deuteronomy 3:8 describes the land Israel took east of the Jordan as running from the Arnon River up to Mount Hermon. So Hermon served as a northern landmark, the edge of the map.

The name Hermon may carry meaning too. It shares its Hebrew root letters, h-r-m, with a word for something set apart or devoted, often to destruction. That word is *herem*. Heiser paid close attention to this link. As the next lesson shows, the book of 1 Enoch plays on it as well.

words.d: the tallest mountain in the region, about 9,200 feet, at the northern edge of the biblical lands
a Hebrew word for something set apart or devoted to God, often to destruction; it shares root letters with Hermon

look.title: How Tall Is Hermon?
look.prompt: About how many times higher than Mount Zion is Hermon? Why would it make a good landmark?

check.q: About how high is Mount Hermon?
check.why: Hermon rises about 9,200 feet. About 2,500 feet is the height of Mount Zion.

check.q: According to Deuteronomy 3:9, what did the Sidonians call Hermon?
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:9 says the Sidonians called it Sirion and the Amorites called it Senir.

check.q: What does the Hebrew word herem refer to?
choices: Something set apart or devoted, often to destruction
check.why: Herem means something devoted or set apart; it shares the root letters h-r-m with Hermon.

lessons.title: Hermon in 1 Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch says the Watchers came down on Mount Hermon and bound themselves there with an oath.
reading: 1 Enoch is an ancient Jewish book made of several parts. Its first part, the *Book of the Watchers*, was probably written by the third century BCE. It is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches. Pieces of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

1 Enoch 6 retells Genesis 6 in much more detail. It says two hundred *Watchers*, heavenly beings, came down in the days of Jared onto the top of Mount Hermon. There they bound themselves together with an *oath*. The text explains the mountain's name from this oath. It is a play on the h-r-m root.

Heiser wrote at length on this passage, especially in Reversing Hermon (2017). He argued that Hermon became, for ancient Jewish readers, a symbol of the rebellion of Genesis 6. That helps explain, in his reading, why the land below it carried a dark reputation. Other scholars read 1 Enoch as a later retelling. For them, it shows how Jews of that time read Genesis, not what Genesis first meant.

words.d: in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down to earth and broke God's order
the first part of 1 Enoch, chapters 1 to 36, probably written by the third century BCE
a solemn promise that binds the people who make it

look.title: The Watchers on Hermon
look.text: In the days of Jared, two hundred of them came down onto the peak of Mount Hermon. They named the mountain Hermon because there they had sworn an oath and bound one another with curses.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 6:6, paraphrased from R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: How does this passage explain the mountain's name? Why might that matter to someone reading about Bashan below it?

check.q: Where does 1 Enoch 6 say the Watchers came down?
choices: On the top of Mount Hermon
check.why: 1 Enoch 6:6 places the Watchers' descent and oath on the peak of Mount Hermon.

check.q: In which churches is 1 Enoch part of the Bible?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

check.q: How do some other scholars read 1 Enoch's Hermon story?
choices: As a chapter of the Masoretic Text
As the oldest book in the Hebrew Bible
As a later retelling that shows how Jews of that time read Genesis
As a record written by Moses
check.why: Many scholars treat 1 Enoch as a later expansion of Genesis 6, useful for how it was read then.

lessons.title: Og's Kingdom
lessons.mainIdea: Joshua 12:4-5 says Og ruled Bashan from Ashtaroth and Edrei up to Mount Hermon, and calls him one of the Rephaim.
reading: Bashan is the high, fertile land east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Today much of it lies in the Golan Heights and southern Syria. Its soil comes from old volcanic rock, which makes it good for grass and grain. In the Bible it is the kingdom of Og.

Joshua 12:4 describes Og as one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at *Ashtaroth* and at *Edrei*. Verse 5 says he ruled in Mount Hermon, in Salcah and in all Bashan. Deuteronomy 3:13 goes further. It says all of Bashan was called the land of the Rephaim.

Israel's victory over Og at Edrei is told in Numbers 21:33-35 and Deuteronomy 3:1-7. Later songs remember it. Psalm 135 and Psalm 136 both list Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, among the kings God defeated. Heiser read the steady focus on Og as a clue that Bashan mattered to the writers for more than its farmland.

words.d: a city of Bashan where Og lived, according to Joshua 12:4
a city of Bashan where Og lived and where Israel defeated his army
the small part of a group that is left over

look.title: Og's Kingdom by the Numbers
rows: Walled cities in the region of Argob (Deuteronomy 3:4)
Amorite kings defeated east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:8)
Length of Og's bed in cubits (Deuteronomy 3:11)
look.prompt: Deuteronomy 3:4 counts sixty walled cities in one part of Og's land. What does that suggest about how strong the writers thought his kingdom was?

check.q: Which two cities does Joshua 12:4 name as Og's home?
check.why: Joshua 12:4 says Og lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 3:13 call the land of Bashan?
choices: The land of milk and honey
check.why: Deuteronomy 3:13 says all Bashan was called the land of the Rephaim.

check.q: Which psalms list Og among the kings God defeated?
check.why: Psalm 135:11 and Psalm 136:20 name Og, king of Bashan.

lessons.title: Ashtaroth and Edrei at Ugarit
lessons.mainIdea: A tablet from Ugarit names a god who dwells in Ashtaroth and rules in Edrei, the same cities as Og's.
reading: Recall Ugarit, the ancient city on the Syrian coast. Its clay tablets were found from 1929 on. One short tablet, catalogued by scholars as KTU 1.108, speaks of a figure called *Rapiu*, king of eternity. Scholars commonly translate a line that says this god dwells in Ashtaroth and rules, or judges, in Edrei.

Those are the very cities of Og in Joshua 12:4. The name Rapiu also comes from the same root as Rephaim. Other *Ugaritic* texts speak of the rpum as the honored dead, especially dead kings. So in Ugarit's world, the area of Ashtaroth and Edrei was tied to the Rephaim and to the realm of the dead.

Heiser saw this as strong background for the Bible. In his reading, an Israelite writer who called Bashan the land of the Rephaim would have known this reputation. Bashan was, in the religious map of Israel's neighbors, a kind of gateway to the underworld. Other scholars agree the match is striking. They are more cautious about how much Israel's writers knew or meant by it.

words.d: the language of Ugarit, written in a wedge-shaped alphabet on clay tablets and close to Hebrew
a figure in a Ugaritic tablet, called king of eternity, whose name shares a root with Rephaim

look.title: A Line From Ugarit
look.text: Let Rapiu, the eternal king, drink: the god who lives in Ashtaroth, the god who rules in Edrei.
look.cite: Ugaritic tablet KTU 1.108, about the 13th century BCE; paraphrased from common scholarly translations
look.prompt: Compare this line with Joshua 12:4. Which words match? Why might a scholar find that exciting?

check.q: Which two place names appear both in Joshua 12:4 and in the tablet KTU 1.108?
check.why: Joshua 12:4 puts Og at Ashtaroth and Edrei, and KTU 1.108 places Rapiu in the same two cities.

check.q: Which word shares a root with the name Rapiu?
check.why: Rapiu and Rephaim come from the same root, which also appears in the Ugaritic word rpum.

check.q: How do some other scholars respond to Heiser's use of this tablet?
choices: They find the match striking but are more cautious about what Israel's writers meant
They say Moses wrote the tablet
They say Ugarit stood in Bashan
They say the tablet mentions Goliath
check.why: Many scholars accept the link between the texts but are careful about what the biblical writers intended.

lessons.title: Bulls, Oaks and a Serpent's Name
lessons.mainIdea: Bashan was famous for strong cattle and oaks, and Heiser noted that its name sounds like an old word for serpent.
reading: Bashan's rich *pastures* made it famous. Amos 4:1 speaks of the cows of Bashan. Ezekiel 39:18 mentions the fattened animals of Bashan. Isaiah 2:13 and Ezekiel 27:6 speak of its oaks. To biblical writers, Bashan meant strength, wealth and plenty.

Psalm 22 uses Bashan in a different way. The speaker is in deep trouble. In verse 12 he says that strong bulls of Bashan have surrounded him. The picture is of powerful enemies closing in. Many Christians read this psalm alongside the story of Jesus's death, since Jesus speaks its first line in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34.

Heiser added a note about language. In Ugaritic, the word for serpent is written btn, which is close to the Hebrew name Bashan. He argued that the name could make ancient readers think of a place of the serpent, which fit Bashan's reputation. Other scholars note the sound link but think the name simply described the land, perhaps as a fertile plain. This kind of sound link is called *wordplay*.

words.d: land covered with grass where animals graze
using a word that sounds like another word to hint at a second meaning

look.title: Three Pictures of Bashan
look.text: Amos 4:1: the cows of Bashan, well fed and comfortable. Isaiah 2:13: the tall oaks of Bashan, proud and strong. Psalm 22:12: the strong bulls of Bashan, closing in around the speaker.
look.prompt: What do all three pictures share? What changes from the first picture to the last?

check.q: Which animals of Bashan does Psalm 22:12 describe?
check.why: Psalm 22:12 says strong bulls of Bashan surround the speaker.

check.q: What was Bashan famous for in texts like Amos 4:1 and Isaiah 2:13?
check.why: Amos speaks of Bashan's cows and Isaiah of its oaks, signs of a rich land.

check.q: What sound link did Heiser point out?
choices: Bashan sounds like the Ugaritic word for serpent
Bashan sounds like the Greek word for giant
Bashan sounds like the Hebrew word for grasshopper
Bashan sounds like the name Hermon
check.why: Heiser noted that Ugaritic btn, serpent, is close to the name Bashan.

lessons.title: Bashan Jealous of Zion
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 68:15–16 pictures Bashan's mountain looking with envy at Zion, the mountain God chose.
reading: Psalm 68 is a victory song. In verses 15 and 16 it turns to mountains. It calls the mountain of Bashan a mountain of God, a mountain of many peaks. Then it asks why the many-peaked mountains look with envy at the mountain God desired for his home.

The mountain God desired is *Zion*, the hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood. Zion is small. At about 2,500 feet it is far lower than Hermon at about 9,200 feet. Yet the psalm says God chose to live on the little hill, not the grand one. Many readers see this as a picture of God choosing the humble over the proud.

Heiser read more in it. The Hebrew word *elohim* can mean God or gods, so the phrase can be read as mountain of gods. He took the peaks of Bashan, likely including Hermon, as the seat of rival powers. In his view the psalm pictures a contest between two holy mountains. Other readers take mountain of God as a Hebrew way of saying a very great mountain.

words.d: the hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood; often a name for Jerusalem itself
a Hebrew word that can mean God, gods, or spiritual beings, depending on the sentence

look.title: Two Mountains in a Psalm
look.text: The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan; an high hill as the hill of Bashan. Why leap ye, ye high hills? this is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the LORD will dwell in it for ever.
look.prompt: The KJV says the hills leap. Many newer translations say they look with envy. How does each word change the picture?

check.q: In Psalm 68:16, which mountain does God desire to dwell in?
check.why: The mountain God desired is Zion in Jerusalem; Bashan's peaks look at it with envy.

check.q: What did Heiser think the mountain of Bashan stood for in this psalm?
choices: The home of the twelve tribes
The seat of rival spiritual powers
The field where David fought Goliath
check.why: Heiser read mountain of gods as pointing to rival powers linked with Bashan and Hermon.

check.q: How do some other readers understand the phrase mountain of God here?
choices: As a copying error for Hebron
As a Hebrew way of saying a very great mountain
As a name for the city of Gath
check.why: Hebrew sometimes uses elohim to mean very great, so mountain of God can mean a mighty mountain.

lessons.title: Heiser's Cosmic Geography
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser used the term cosmic geography for the biblical idea that places on earth were linked to spiritual powers.
reading: In 1 Samuel 26:19, David is on the run from King Saul. He complains that he has been driven out of the LORD's *inheritance*, as if told to go and serve other gods. In 2 Kings 5:17, Naaman, an army commander from Aram, has met the prophet Elisha. Before going home, he asks for two mules' loads of Israel's soil, so he can worship Israel's God on it.

Heiser saw a pattern in stories like these. He called it *cosmic geography*: the belief that land was also spiritual territory. He followed the Dead Sea Scrolls reading of Deuteronomy 32:8-9. It says God divided the nations by the number of the sons of God. God kept Israel as his own. So, in his reading, Israel's land was holy ground, and other lands were seen as the domains of other gods.

Bashan and Hermon fit this map, in Heiser's view. They sat at the edge of Israel's land and were linked with the Rephaim, the dead and the Watchers. Other scholars see stories like Naaman's as showing common ancient ideas about local gods. They think Israel's writers used those ideas without building a full system. Either way, place mattered in these texts.

words.d: Heiser's term for the biblical idea that places on earth were linked to spiritual powers
in these texts, the land or people that belong to God as his own share

look.title: Naaman's Soil
look.text: Naaman is a powerful army commander from Aram, a kingdom north of Israel. After his visit to Elisha, he does something surprising. He asks for two mules' loads of dirt to carry home. He wants to worship Israel's God there, standing on Israel's ground (2 Kings 5:17).
look.prompt: Why would Naaman want dirt from Israel? What does it suggest about how he thought gods and lands were connected?

check.q: What did Naaman ask to take home in 2 Kings 5:17?
choices: Stones from the Valley of Elah
Two mules' loads of soil from Israel
check.why: Naaman asked for two mules' loads of Israel's soil so he could worship Israel's God on it.

check.q: What does cosmic geography mean in Heiser's work?
choices: The study of stars and planets
The idea that places on earth were linked to spiritual powers
check.why: Heiser used cosmic geography for the belief that land was also spiritual territory.

check.q: Which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 does Heiser's view follow?
choices: The Masoretic reading, sons of Israel
A reading that says sons of Anak
The Dead Sea Scrolls reading, sons of God
A reading that says sons of Bashan
check.why: Heiser followed the Dead Sea Scrolls reading, sons of God; the Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel.

sections.title: The Conquest and Its Hard Questions

lessons.title: Aimed at the Giant Clans
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that the conquest stories focus on the giant clans, and saw them as a key reason for the conquest.
reading: Deuteronomy 9:1-2 prepares Israel to cross the Jordan. It warns of great walled cities and a people tall like the Anakim. It quotes a saying: who can stand before the sons of Anak? Joshua 11:21-22 then reports that Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country. The giant clans are named at the start of the *conquest* and near its end.

The books use a strong word for this war: herem, the ban. It meant devoting a city and its people to God by destruction. Deuteronomy 2:34 and 3:6 use it for the cities of Sihon and Og, east of the Jordan. Joshua uses it for Jericho and other towns.

Heiser argued the ban was aimed especially at the places where the giant clans lived. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he read the conquest partly as a campaign. It was aimed at the peoples the writers tied to Genesis 6. He noticed that the same places come up again and again: Hebron, Gath and Bashan. Other scholars read the giant language as one theme among several, beside land, covenant loyalty and worship.

words.d: taking land by force; here, the stories in Numbers, Deuteronomy and Joshua of Israel entering Canaan
the usual English name for herem: devoting a city and its people to God by destruction

look.title: Giant Clans Across the Conquest
look.text: Numbers 13:33: the scouts see the sons of Anak. Deuteronomy 2:10-11 and 2:20-21: Emim and Zamzummim, counted as Rephaim. Deuteronomy 3:11: Og, last of the Rephaim. Deuteronomy 9:2: who can stand before the sons of Anak? Joshua 11:21-22: the Anakim removed, except in three cities. Joshua 15:14: Caleb takes Hebron.
look.prompt: Look at where the giant clans appear. Why might Heiser say they are a key theme, and why might another scholar call them one theme among several?

check.q: What saying does Deuteronomy 9:2 quote?
choices: Who can stand before the sons of Anak?
Only Og remained of the Rephaim
The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan
check.why: Deuteronomy 9:2 quotes the saying about standing before the sons of Anak; the grasshoppers come from Numbers 13:33.

check.q: What is herem in the conquest stories?
choices: The ban: devoting a city and its people to God by destruction
check.why: Herem, the ban, means devoting a city and its people to God by destruction, as in Deuteronomy 2:34.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about the conquest?
choices: It was aimed in part at the giant clans tied to Genesis 6
check.why: In The Unseen Realm (2015), Heiser read the ban as aimed especially at the giant clans.

lessons.title: Naming the Hard Questions
lessons.mainIdea: The conquest texts describe the destruction of whole towns, and Jewish and Christian readers have long wrestled with them.
reading: These texts are hard to read. Deuteronomy 2:34 says Israel devoted the towns of Sihon to destruction, men, women and children, leaving none. Joshua 6:21 says the same of Jericho. Many readers, religious and not, find these words deeply troubling. Honest study names that plainly.

The Bible itself adds details that complicate the picture. Rahab of Jericho and her family are spared and live on in Israel (Joshua 6:25). The *Gibeonites* make a treaty and are kept alive (Joshua 9). Genesis 15:16 says the land would be given only when the wrongdoing of the Amorites was complete. Some readers take that as a long delay before judgment.

Jewish readers have wrestled with these texts for centuries. An old tradition, found in the Jerusalem Talmud and in midrash, says Joshua first sent word offering peace or the chance to leave. The medieval teacher *Maimonides* wrote that those ancient nations no longer exist, so the command cannot apply to anyone today. Many Christian readers see the conquest as a one-time judgment in a unique moment. Others, like the early teacher *Origen*, read the battles as pictures of inner, spiritual struggles.

Heiser's giant-clan reading is one more attempt to explain why these texts single out certain peoples. Some readers find it helpful. Others say it still leaves the hardest question, the harm to families and children. Students can set these readings side by side and discuss them with care.

look.title: Four Ways Readers Respond
look.text: 1. Peace first: an old Jewish tradition says Joshua offered peace or a chance to leave. 2. No longer in force: Maimonides wrote that the ancient nations are gone, so the command applies to no one today. 3. A one-time judgment: many Christians read it as unique to that time. 4. An inner battle: Origen read the wars as pictures of spiritual struggle.

lessons.title: Ancient War Writing and Hyperbole
lessons.mainIdea: Some scholars read the conquest reports as hyperbole, a common style in ancient war writing.
reading: Around 840 BCE, King Mesha of Moab set up a stone to celebrate his victories. The *Mesha Stele* is now in the Louvre museum in Paris. It boasts that Israel had perished forever. Yet Israel did not perish. The claim is hyperbole, an overstatement meant to praise a king and his god. The stele even uses a word from the same root as herem.

Some scholars have compared Joshua with war reports from Assyria, Egypt and the Hittites. K. Lawson Younger did this in his 1990 study, Ancient Conquest Accounts. Such scholars found the same patterns: victories that sound total, repeated set phrases and huge numbers. On this reading, words like leaving none alive were a standard way to say a battle was won.

The Bible's own pages give hints. Joshua 10:40 says Joshua left none remaining in the south. But Joshua 15:14 and Judges 1:10 say Hebron still had to be taken. Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in three cities. Readers who hold the hyperbole view point to such differences. Heiser's reading uses the same verses about survivors, since they explain the giants of Gath.

an upright stone slab carved with writing, often to honor a ruler

look.title: A King's Boast in Stone
look.text: King Mesha says that Omri's son, the king of Israel, meant to crush Moab. But Mesha says he won, and he boasts that Israel has perished forever.
